title: Contextualizing Misinformation: A User-Centric Approach to Linguistic and Topical Patterns in News Consumption
screen_reason: The paper's aim is linguistic (readability, sentiment, morality, perplexity of consumed misinformation), which on its own would be excluded, but Section 4 opens with topline descriptive behavioural REACH statistics: the percentage of panelists who visited at least one misinformation article in each of four topical categories (12.7% U.S. electoral politics, 10.9% social issues, 6.7% COVID-19, 4.3% health), from passively logged web-browsing of a nationally representative YouGov Pulse panel. These are quantitative shares of people reached at least once, with a stated denominator (1,240 participants), so the paper is included on those rows.

estimates.platform: Web browsing (desktop/laptop, smartphone, tablet URL visits; YouGov Pulse)
estimates.measure_type: % of panelists who visited at least one U.S. electoral politics misinformation article
estimates.denominator: 1,240 American adults in a nationally representative YouGov panel with passive web-tracking (YouGov Pulse), weighted to the US adult population
estimates.definition: A participant counted in the numerator if their tracked browsing contained at least one visit to an article on a misinformation domain that GPT-4o mini classified as U.S. Electoral Politics.
estimates.misinfo_def: "For misinformation, we follow Nyhan and Reifler [124], who define it as 'information that is false, misleading, or unsubstantiated.'"
estimates.source_quote: We found that the most consumed type of misinformation articles was about U.S. Electoral Politics, with 12.7% (95% CI [10.9, 14.7]) of participants being exposed to at least one such article.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Domain-level classification taken from Dahlke et al. [38]: NewsGuard ratings of sites that "repeatedly publish false content" combined with the academic lists of Guess et al. [64] and Allcott et al. [4], giving 1,796 unique misinformation domains; hard news = Bakshy et al. [13] plus 5,471 NewsGuard-rated sites that do not repeatedly publish false content. Topic labels assigned by GPT-4o mini after inductive stm topic modelling; validated on a random 100 articles against two independent human coders, Cohen's kappa = 0.76.
estimates.moderator_quote: Fig. 5. Descriptive results of topline levels of exposure among the 1,240 participants by misinformation and hard news topics. ... The y-axis is the percentage of participants who were exposed to at least one article of each topic.
estimates.notes: Reach is topic-specific: the four extracted rows partition misinformation exposure by topic and MUST NOT be summed (one person can be reached on several topics) and no all-topic misinformation reach figure is stated anywhere in the text. Denominator: the Figure 5 caption states the 1,240 panelists; the regression samples use the 719 participants who visited at least one misinformation or hard news page, so the descriptive denominator (1,240) is the wider one, as stated. Domain-level classification means a whole site's articles are treated as misinformation, so breadth is blank per the source-list rule.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) General News misinformation reach is plotted in Figure 5 as a fifth category but no numeric value appears in the text, so it cannot be extracted without reading the figure - if the review wants it, it needs the figure or the replication data. (2) An EXPOSURE diet-share statement exists but is an eyeballed description of Figure 3 rather than a stated value: 'There was a notable build-up in electoral politics misinformation preceding Election Day 2020, with the percentage rising from around 2-3% pre-election to peaks of nearly 6% of total articles (misinformation plus hard news) just before the election and in the weeks after.' I did not create a row: 'around 2-3%' and 'nearly 6%' are approximations read off a figure, they are topic-restricted (electoral politics only, not all misinformation), and the denominator is only misinformation-plus-hard-news articles rather than all browsing. An adjudicator who wants a news-diet share for this study could enter it as value_kind range_not_point, EXPOSURE / diet_share, denom_scope news_diet. (3) No overall 'share of URL visits that were misinformation' is reported: the paper gives 21M total URL visits and 91,424 unique misinformation + hard news URLs, but never the misinformation/hard-news split of either, so no exposure proportion is derivable. (4) All linguistic results (readability, sentiment, morality, perplexity; Tables 1-4, Figures 6-9) are regression coefficients on continuous scales, not shares - no rows. (5) Demographic contrasts (older adults consume more COVID-19/health misinformation, Republicans more social-issues and electoral misinformation) are interaction coefficients on topic probabilities, not shares of people or items - no rows. (6) Sample-composition percentages (29.2% aged 65+, 31.4% Republican, etc.) describe the panel, not misinformation.

rob.design: Two-wave YouGov survey plus passive web-tracking (YouGov Pulse) of every URL visited on desktop/laptop, smartphone and tablet, 24 August - 7 December 2020; N = 1,240 nationally representative American adults (weights supplied and used), 21M URL visits; 719 participants visited at least one misinformation or hard news page and form the modelling sample. Misinformation and hard news assigned at the DOMAIN level from Dahlke et al. (NewsGuard 'repeatedly publishes false content' plus Guess et al. and Allcott et al.; 1,796 misinformation domains), dynamic pages removed and query strings stripped, article text scraped with headless Chrome, giving 91,424 unique URLs. Topics from inductive stm modelling then GPT-4o mini zero-shot labelling, validated on 100 random articles against two independent human coders (Cohen's kappa = 0.76). Response rate not reported; partisanship and age are self-reported (robustness check in Appendix C). Authors flag domain-level labelling as their main measurement limitation.
